# A Simple Circuit for Time-Resolved Luminescence (TRL) Measurement Instruments: Demonstration Through a Smartphone-Based TRL Imager for Anticounterfeiting Application

**Authors:** Alim Gulbag; Michael Huang; Brian Rong; Benjamin Sreenan; Xiaoshan Zhu

**Affiliations:** Department of Electrical and Biomedical Engineering, University of Nevada Reno, NV 98557 USA

## Abstract

Time-resolved luminescence (TRL) measurement is a sensitive detection technique by eliminating sample autofluorescence, but TRL measurement instruments composed of multiple key components (e.g., a rapidly pulsed light excitation source, a time-gated optical detector, and a synchronization module aligning the timing between the light source and the detector) have been sophisticated, expensive, or bulky, which limits their point-of-care or in-field applications. To reduce the cost and complexity of these instruments, in this work, we developed a simple circuit for rapid LED pulsing and accurate timing synchronization, and implemented it in a compact TRL imager with a UV LED as light source and a chopper-coupled smartphone camera as time-gated optical detector. The TRL measurement of this imager using this circuit was successfully validated through an anticounterfeiting application. We believe that this simple circuit can be adopted in the development of low-cost and compact TRL measurement instruments for broad point-of-care or in-field applications.

## INTRODUCTION

Time-resolved luminescence (TRL) measurement, utilizing long-lived-luminescence materials (e.g., lanthanide-based complexes, manganese (Mn)-doped nanocrystals), is a sensitive detection technique [1]. In this technique, after pulsed excitation, sample autofluorescence decays within tens of nanoseconds, but these materials still emit long-lasting luminescence for signal measurement. Due to its high signal-to-background (S/B) ratio, this technique has gained wide applications in anticounterfeiting, sensing, and imaging [1–2]. Despite its effectiveness in sensitive detection, the instruments for TRL measurement are generally complex involving multiple components (e.g., a rapidly pulsed light excitation source, a high-speed time-gated optical detector, and a synchronization module aligning the timing between the light source and the detector) [2]. Moreover, some components such as photodetectors and synchronization modules are expensive or bulky. As a result, large, complicated, and costly instruments usually are developed for laboratory use, and the point-of-care or in-field applications of TRL measurement have been limited. With the recent technology advance in light excitation sources (e.g., high-power UV LEDs), mechanical chopper-based optical detector, and manufacturing, compact instruments have been reported [3–4]. But electronic circuits for timing synchronization as well as light source pulsing were still sophisticated in these systems. For instance, these systems used either a digital delay generator (e.g., DG535, > $4,000, Stanford Research System) or FGPA/MCU programming for synchronization and light pulsing, which are expensive, or complex/time-consuming in development. To develop low-cost and miniaturized TRL instruments for potential point-of-care or in-field applications, simple, cheap, and compact circuits are highly needed.

In this work, we developed a simple circuit using dual retriggerable monostable multivibrators and several additional components for timing synchronization and LED pulsing, which costs less than $40 and is easy to tune. We implemented this circuit in a compact TRL imager with a UV LED (up to 1 W optical output power) as light source and a chopper-coupled smartphone camera as time-gated optical detector. Using Mn-doped nanocrystals (NCs) as long-lived-luminescence materials (luminescence lifetime at ~ 2 ms) [5], we demonstrated that this imager using this circuit functioned properly for its TRL measurement in an anticounterfeiting application. We believe that this simple circuit can be adopted in the development of low-cost and compact TRL measurement instruments using materials with luminescence lifetimes at milli-second levels for broad point-of-care or in-field applications.

## EXPERIMENTAL

### Materials and Apparatus

A mechanical optical chopper with a controller (MC2000B) was from Thorlabs. LEDs (ELUA3535NU3, ~ 400 nm emission, 1 W optical output), dual retriggerable monostable multivibrators (SN74AHC123AN), and other electronics parts were from Digikey or Mouser. A smartphone (iPhone 15) was from Apple. Adhesive films were from USA Scientific. Organic solvent Tetrahydrofuran (THF) and glass slides were from VWR. Mn-doped and undoped NCs (Mn:AgZnInS/ZnS and AgZnInS/ZnS NCs) were prepared using a previous method [5]. All mechanical parts were prepared through 3D printing. Oscilloscope Tektronix TDS-2012B 100 MHZ and Hamamatsu photomultiplier tube (PMT) H10721–20 with related components were used in experiments for circuit characterization. Image J, an open-source image processing program developed at the National Institutes of Health, was used for image analysis.

### Imaging Experiments and Image Analysis

After an adhesive film was cut with 2-mm through-holes using laser, it adhered to a glass slide. Then, 3 μL of Mn-doped NCs dissolved in THF with a concentration (e.g., 100 μg/mL) was pipetted to a through-hole or a well. After THF evaporated, the adhesive film was peeled off, and a spot of Mn-doped NCs was deposited on the glass slide for TRL measurement. Each testing condition was repeated in triplicates. For anticounterfeiting application, an array of 2 × 3 through-holes on a glass slide were deposited with undoped NCs (1 mg/mL, luminescence lifetime < 1 μs) and then some selected through-holes (or wells) were further deposited with Mn-doped NCs. After dry and film peel-off, the glass slide was imaged under time-resolved mode and non-time-resolved mode. For image analysis, we took multiple images for each testing condition. For the region of interests (i.e., NC-deposited spot) in the images, we used Z-stack to get the Z-stack mean of all images and then averaged all these values to achieve a new mean value with a standard deviation. The reason to use Z-stack is that NCs are not evenly distributed in each well due to solvent surface tension during THF evaporation. Triplicate averaging produced a final average with a standard deviation. The S/B ratio was calculated as the ratio between the mean value for a certain Mn-doped NC concentration and the mean value for a blank glass. No additional processes like brightness or contrast enhancement were applied to the images, considering possible in-field applications.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Overview of TRL, the Circuit, and the TRL Imager

TRL measurement using a pulsed LED excitation source and an optical chopper-based camera has two basic steps, as shown in Fig. 1(A). First, LED is turned on for sample excitation. In the excitation phase, Mn-doped NCs and sample matrix will produce signal and background, respectively. But the camera will be blocked by the chopper blade, and no signal and background can be read by camera. Second, after LED is turned off, with a certain time delay, sample autofluorescence fades out quickly due to its short lifetime, but Mn-doped NCs still emit the signal due to their long luminescence lifetime at ~ 2 ms. Then, the chopper blade is rotated away or opened, so that the camera records the signal only. TRL measurement thus naturally has a high S/B ratio. In this system, the chopper is controlled by a controller which also provides a reference-output (a frequency clock aligned with the rotation speed of chopper). To ensure TRL measurement, the timing synchronization between the pulsed LED and the chopper reference-output is critical and needs to be manually tuned, so that no excitation light leak from the LED into the camera. It is noted that the camera blocking/opening status is not exactly aligned with the falling or rising edge of the chopper reference-output due to the size of pinhole for camera recording, the positioning between the camera and the chopper, and so on [3]. In other words, at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, the camera could be blocked or opened. For such uncertain circumstances, Fig. 1(B) illustrates our proposed method for timing synchronization – the falling edge of the chopper reference-output triggers a tunable pulse (defined as the delay pulse (Pdelay)), and the falling edge of the delay pulse then triggers another tunable pulse (defined as the LED pulse) to turn on LED with a certain pulsing width (Pwidth). If the camera is opened at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, Pdelay can be tuned long enough until the camera is blocked and then LED is triggered to turn on for excitation. After LED is on, Pwidth of LED should be tuned in an appropriate range to avoid LED light leaking into the camera (i.e., LED should be turned off before the camera is opened again). Oppositely, if the camera is blocked at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, Pdelay can be set at its minimum value, and Pwidth of LED is thus tuned in an appropriate range for excitation.

Different from conventional digital delay generators or FPGA/MCU programming for timing synchronization and LED pulsing, our circuit simply uses low-cost dual retriggerable monostable multivibrators and several additional components, and its schematic is presented in Fig. 1(C). With a multivibrator, the falling edge of the chopper reference-output is used to trigger a pulse (the delay pulse in Fig. 1(B)). With another multivibrator, the falling edge of the delay pulse is used to trigger another pulse (the LED pulse in Figure 1(B)). The pulse time (Pdelay) of the delay pulse and the pulse time (Pwidth) of the LED pulse are determined by a pair of external potentiometers and capacitors, allowing for fine tuning of output durations (τ = R × C). Potentiometers and capacitors were selected in this work to tune these two time-parameters in the range of 10 μs to 2 ms. Appropriate components can be chosen for broader time tuning, depending on specific applications. In this circuit, the LED pulse is fed into a LED driver to rapidly pulse a UV LED. The LED driver essentially is an inverter (a pair of NMOSFET and PMOSFET) with LED as load. The NMOS (IRF540) and PMOS (IRF9Z34N) pair works like a conventional CMOS inverter in a push-pull mode to turn on and off LED, respectively. Note that both MOSFETs are of high-speeds (< 55 ns turn on/off dynamic times) and low turn-on resistances (~ 0.1 ohms), which will facilitate the rapid pulsing of LED. A 5.6 ohms resistor is connected between the drain of PMOS and the drain of NMOS (or the LED anode), which is used to set the LED turn-on current at ~ 200 mA for ~ 200 mW optical output and also limit the transient current from power supply to ground through two MOSFETs during switching.

Fig. 1(D) shows the implementation of this circuit into a compact TRL imager with a chopper-based smartphone and a UV LED. 3D printing was used for the preparation of all other parts.

### Circuit Characterization

Fig. 2(A) shows the timing demonstration of the dual multivibrators with the chopper reference-output as the input and the delay pulse and the LED pulse as the outputs. In this demonstration, at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, the delay pulse goes high and lasts for 10μs (Pdelay). At the falling edge of the delay pulse, the LED pulse goes high for 1.9 ms (Pwidth) and turns off before the chopper reference-output goes high. Both Pdelay and Pwidth can be further tuned to different values through the potentiometers.

To test the light switching dynamics of LED and the LED light-output stability over continuous pulsing through the LED driver, a PMT H10721–20 was used to detect the light dynamics and intensity of LED [6]. Fig. 2(B–C) show the rising and falling dynamics of the light from LED with an electrical turn-on or -off control. The rising time and the rising delay time are 0.16 μs and 0.51 μs, respectively. The falling time and the falling delay time are 0.34 μs and 1.23 μs, respectively. Fig. 2(D) shows the normalized LED output-light stability over four hours under different pulsing conditions (250, 500, and 1000 kHz with 50% duty cycles). Each data point in Fig. 2(D) has a relative standard deviation less than 0.03%. Under each testing condition, the relative signal variation over time is no more than 0.08%. No obvious photobleaching of Mn-doped NCs was observed for all tested LED pulsing conditions. From the LED testing data, it can be concluded that the LED driver is able to turn LED on or off fast enough and thus do not affect the chopper-based smartphone to capture the Mn-doped NC luminescence (lasting around 2 ms).

### Optimization of TRL Imaging Through Circuit Tuning

After all the components in the TRL imager (Fig. 1(D)) were properly assembled, the synchronization between the LED excitation source and the chopper-coupled smartphone camera was elaborately carried out to ensure the maximum S/B ratio for TRL imaging [3].

The optimization strategy of synchronization is that for the chopper driven under a certain frequency saying 250 Hz (2 ms on and 2 ms off in a period), the sum of Pdelay and Pwidth (Pdelay + Pwidth) was fixed at a value (illustrated in Fig. 3(A)). For the fixed sum value, Pwidth was tuned from low to high, and meanwhile, and Pdelay was tuned from high to low. Under each synchronization condition, 100 mg/mL and 0 mg/mL Mn-doped NCs deposited on glass were imaged as signal and background, respectively, and the S/B ratio was calculated. Figure 3 (B–D) show the signal, the background, and their S/B ratio under each testing condition (labeled by the value of Pwidth), when the sum (Pdelay + Pwidth) was set at 440, 880, and 1320 μs, respectively. These three sums are representative values from low to high, in order to examine the effectiveness of our optimization strategy. For each fixed sum, the S/B ratio increases versus the Pwidth and then reach a relative saturation plateau. Moreover, the S/B ratio is enhanced as the sum increases. The maximum S/B ratio (~ 37) was achieved with Pwidth = 1310 μs and Pdelay = 10 μs (the sum = 1320 μs). This is reasonable because a long LED pulse will excite Mn-doped NCs with more energy and the NCs will emit more intense luminescence after LED is turned off. Additionally, with Pwidth = 1310 μs, the delay between LED-off and camera-on is shortest, and thus the camera will catch a stronger signal (the delay is longer as the sum is set at 440 μs or 880 μs, and thus the camera will catch a much-delayed low signal after LED is turned off). Note that with Pdelay = 10 μs, when Pwidth was further increased from 1310 μs to a higher value, the blue UV light from LED was observed to leak into the camera. Thus, Pwidth = 1310 μs and Pdelay = 10 μs is considered as the optimal synchronization condition for 250 Hz. Fig.3 (E) presents the TRL images of 100 μg/mL Mn-doped NCs spotted on glass under different Pwidth values when (Pdelay + Pwidth) is set at 1320 μs. It should be mentioned that the luminescence of the same NC sample under non-time-resolved mode (measuring under continuous excitation) is almost hidden under the autofluorescence from glass and/or sample holder (with a S/B ratio of 1.2, the image not shown).

The same strategy was applied for the chopper driven under different frequencies (i.e., 500 and 1000 Hz). The maximum S/B ratios are ~ 34 and ~ 31 for 500 Hz and 1000 Hz, respectively. Through the comparison among all S/B ratios, Pdelay = 10 μs and Pwidth = 1310 μs under 250 Hz achieved the best S/B ratio and was thus selected as the optimal condition for TRL imaging.

### Anticounterfeiting Application

With the optimal imaging condition, a series of Mn-doped NC solutions with different concentrations were prepared and deposited on glass slides for TRL imaging. Fig. 4(A) shows representative TRL images for different Mn-doped NC concentrations. Fig. 4(B) presents the calibration curve of the TRL intensity of a spot versus the concentration of Mn-doped NCs deposited in the spot. Based on Fig.4(B), the limit of detection (LOD) of Mn-doped NCs is calculated to be around 1.4 μg/mL using the 3-sigma method. Although this low LOD indicates the high sensitivity of the optimized TRL instrument, for the anticounterfeiting application, to save the analysis time and the material cost, a middle-level concentration of Mn-doped NCs with a confidently recognizable intensity by human eye-vision is preferred. Thus, Mn-doped NCs at 50 μg/mL were used in anticounterfeiting application. Fig. 4(C–D) present the imaging of the specific patterns (left and right pointing triangles) of Mn-doped NCs deposited in a 2 × 3 array of wells with undoped NCs as backgrounds. Under continuous excitation (non-time-resolved mode), all wells present orange luminescence and the specific patterns for anticounterfeiting are hidden. Only under TRL measurement, the luminescence of undoped NCs is not measurable due to its short luminescence lifetime (< 1 μs), but the specific patterns from the luminescence of Mn-doped NCs (~ 2 ms luminescence lifetime) can be identified. In this application, the specific patterns in a 2 × 3 array of wells are relatively simple, but we believe that if the ink-printing technology is adopted for NC printing, more complex and dense patterns can be printed to enhance the anticounterfeiting coding information.

## CONCLUSION

In this work, we developed a simple circuit for LED pulsing and timing synchronization, and implemented it in a TRL imager with a UV LED as light source and a chopper-coupled smartphone camera as time-gated optical detector. With circuit-parameter tuning for optimization, the TRL measurement of this imager using this circuit was successfully validated through an anticounterfeiting application using Mn-doped NCs. We believe that this simple circuit can be adopted in the development of point-of-care or in-field TRL measurement instruments for broad applications.
